title: How I Paid Off $38,000 in 26 Months
creator: Nina Brooks
description:
Four credit cards, a car loan and one very embarrassing store card. Here's every month of it, including the bad ones.

Next video: the exact budget percentages I used.

I'm not a financial advisor, this is just what worked for me.

sentences.t: Twenty-six months ago I had thirty-eight thousand dollars of debt across four credit cards, a car loan, and one very embarrassing store card.
Today it's zero, and in this video I'm going to show you exactly how that happened, including the months where it didn't go well.
Before the numbers, let me show you the one tool I'd tell my past self to download on day one.
It's called Ledgerleaf, and it connects to your bank accounts and cards and sorts every transaction into categories automatically, so you're not typing in receipts at midnight.
The feature that changed things for me is the debt planner, where you put in every balance and interest rate and it builds you a payoff schedule with an actual date at the end.
Seeing a date, like a real month and year, made the whole thing feel finite instead of endless.
It's also built for couples, so if you share finances you can both see the same budget without sending each other screenshots.
If you go to ledgerleaf.app slash nina, you get your first sixty days completely free, no card needed.
Okay, so here's where I started.
Card one had about eleven thousand on it at twenty-four percent, and that was the scary one.
Cards two and three were smaller, around four thousand each, and the store card was nine hundred dollars that I had honestly forgotten about.
The car loan was the rest, at a much lower rate.
I used what people call the avalanche method, which means you pay minimums on everything and throw every extra dollar at the highest interest rate first.
Mathematically, that saves you the most money.
Emotionally, it's brutal, because that first balance takes forever to move.
So I made one exception, and I paid off the nine hundred dollar store card first, just to get a win.
Was that optimal?
No.
Did it keep me going?
Absolutely.
The second big change was income, not spending.
I was cutting coffee and canceling streaming and it was saving me maybe eighty dollars a month, which is real, but it's not going to kill thirty-eight thousand dollars.
What actually moved the needle was asking for a raise, which I'd been too scared to do for two years, and picking up weekend tutoring.
That added about seven hundred a month, and all of it went straight to debt.
Months nine through twelve were the worst.
My car needed a new transmission, I had to put some of it back on a card, and I cried in a grocery store parking lot.
I'm telling you that because so many payoff videos make it look like a straight line, and it isn't.
But by month eighteen, card one was gone, and after that everything snowballed, because all that money freed up at once.
The car loan was the last thing, I paid it off two months ago, and I took a very small, very cheap trip to celebrate.
If you're at the start of this, the one thing I'd say is, write the number down, look at it, and pick a date.
In the next video I'll go through the exact budget percentages I used each month.
Leave your questions below and I'll answer as many as I can.
